title: Gaudete Sunday (Philippians 4:4)
hook: the rose candle: rejoice, the Lord is near

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nican Mopohua: roses in December and a question that's also a promise, am I not here. Who showed up for you, or did you show up for? Day six hundred thirty-seven.

Look at an Advent wreath in its third week. Two purple candles have burned down a little. Then there's one that isn't purple at all. It's pink, or as the Church calls it, rose. On the third Sunday of Advent the priest may wear rose vestments too, a color that appears only twice a year. People who don't know the reason sometimes think the florist got the order wrong. The real reason is one Latin word, the first word sung at that Sunday's Mass for many centuries. Today's word.
screen: `TWO PURPLE, THEN ONE ROSE.` → `ONLY TWICE A YEAR.` → `ONE LATIN WORD.`

segments.voice: Gaudete means rejoice, said to more than one person. It opens the entrance chant of the third Sunday of Advent, taken from Paul's letter to the Philippians. In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice." And the reason follows a verse later: "The Lord is nigh." Here's what gives it weight. Paul wrote this letter in chains. He mentions his bonds again and again, and he isn't sure he'll leave prison alive. So this isn't a cheerful man telling everyone to smile. It's a prisoner insisting that joy has a source outside his circumstances. Advent is a season of waiting, and waiting can turn grim. So halfway through, the Church lightens the color. Purple softens to rose, as if the first light of dawn were showing at the edge of the sky. It isn't Christmas yet. The waiting isn't over. But the nearness has started to show. Gaudete Sunday ends a week that has walked a long way. It opened with the Bible's last prayer, Maranatha, take the water of life, freely. Then we learned that every day has a rank. The new year began with one word, watch. Isaiah gave us a great light. Kecharitomene gave us full of grace from the start. Guadalupe gave us am I not here. And now rose, and rejoice. Read them in a row and they form a small Advent all their own: a cry, a calendar, a lookout, a light, a girl, a mother, and joy on the way.
screen: `GAUDETE: REJOICE, ALL OF YOU.` · `WRITTEN IN CHAINS.` · `PURPLE SOFTENS TO ROSE.` · `A WEEK OF ADVENT, LOOKED BACK.` · then, large: `THE LORD IS NIGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wear something bright. Before you sit, if you can, put on one bright thing: a scarf, a pair of socks, a ring, a pink shirt you never wear. Then sit with it on. Notice one honest reason for joy today, even small, even alongside something hard, the way Paul found his in chains. Don't force a feeling. Just name the reason. If you pray, you can say Paul's words, rejoice in the Lord always. If you don't, simply let the color remind you. The bell holds the time.
Gaudete. Latin for rejoice, said to many. It names the third Sunday of Advent, with its rose candle and rose vestments. Today's word.
Your line: rejoice. Today, wear your bright thing where someone can see it, and if they ask, tell them it's Gaudete. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: On the third Sunday of Advent many Catholic parishes light the rose candle of the Advent wreath, and the priest may wear rose vestments instead of violet.

to come and break you out.

original.note: Latin: rejoice (to many), the first word of the entrance chant for the third Sunday of Advent.

trapdoor: what you thought: the pink candle is just decoration.
what it means: the rose candle marks Gaudete Sunday, joy halfway through the Advent wait.
what a scholar hears: the introit 'Gaudete in Domino semper' takes Philippians 4:4–5, a letter Paul wrote as a prisoner.

notes: Rose vestments are optional on Gaudete and Laetare Sundays; 'a color that appears only twice a year' refers to these two Sundays. Confirm.
Place of Paul's imprisonment when writing Philippians (Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea) is debated; the script says only 'in chains'.
10% audit (2026-10-01): the look-back said 'last week ended with' Maranatha, but Come, Lord Jesus is day 631, the first day of this week; now 'it opened with'.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Philippians 4:4 and 4:5.
